sentences.text: The scientific validity of several of the ten described species of Dunkleosteus is currently unclear.
D. terrelli is the largest and best-known species of Dunkleosteus and serves as the type species, which is the specimen the species is based on.

Because the body shape is unknown, estimates for the largest known specimen of D. terrelli range from 4.1 to 10 meters in length and 1 to 4 metric tons in weight, though current evidence suggests D. terrelli was likely less than 5 meters long, with recent studies estimating typical adults at approximately 3.4 meters and exceptionally large individuals at 4.1 meters.
Dunkleosteus fossils were first discovered in 1867 by Jay Terrell, an amateur paleontologist who collected them in cliffs near Sheffield Lake, Ohio.
In 1873, John Strong Newberry and the Ohio Geological Survey described Terrell's initial fossils as a single species, Dinichthys herzeri.
By 1875, further discoveries revealed that multiple large fish species existed in the Ohio Shale.
The genus Dunkleosteus was formally described by Lehman in 1956.
Dunkleosteus was a pelagic fish that inhabited open waters and served as one of the first vertebrate apex predators in any ecosystem.
It has been suggested that Dunkleosteus could rapidly open and close its jaws to create suction and possessed an extremely high bite force, though these claims have recently been questioned.

Extensive analyses estimate typical adult Dunkleosteus terrelli at about 3.4 meters, with rare individuals potentially reaching 4.1 meters, while a 2010 study estimated a 4.6-meter adult Dunkleosteus terrelli weighed 665 kg based on a shark-like body plan.
Dunkleosteus was originally thought to belong to the genus Dinichthys but was recognized as a distinct genus in 1956.
Dunkleosteus and Dinichthys were historically grouped together in the family Dinichthyidae.
A 2010 phylogenetic analysis by Carr and Hlavin found that Dunkleosteus and Dinichthys belong to separate clades: Dunkleosteoidea and Aspinothoracidi, respectively.
Carr and Hlavin resurrected the family Dunkleosteidae to include Dunkleosteus and Eastmanosteus along with other genera formerly in Dinichthyidae.
Dunkleosteus lived during the Late Devonian period, specifically from the Frasnian to the Famennian stages.
Fossils of Dunkleosteus have been discovered in the United States, Canada, Poland, Belgium, Morocco, and Russia.
D. marsaisi refers to fossils found in Lower Famennian Late Devonian strata of the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.
D. missouriensis is known from fragments found in Frasnian strata in Missouri.
Lelièvre (1982) considered D. belgicus a doubtful name and suggested the material might actually belong to Ardennosteus.
Many researchers consider D. marsaisi a synonym of D. terrelli, while H. Schultze regards it as a member of Eastmanosteus.
Hlavin (1976) considered D. missouriensis to be tentatively synonymous with D. terrelli.
Only four species are agreed upon as valid by all researchers: D. terrelli, D. raveri, D. tuderensis, and possibly D. amblyodoratus, while the taxonomy of other species remains debated.
